name: gnmic
why: A gNMI client for streaming telemetry from network gear, a door into the OpenConfig protocol routers speak.

brief.what_it_is: gnmic is an open-source gNMI command-line client written in Go, maintained under the OpenConfig project. You point it at a network device's gRPC gNMI endpoint and it can run Capabilities, Get, Set and Subscribe RPCs against that device. It can also run as a collector that takes gNMI telemetry streams from many targets, processes them, and writes them to outputs such as Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, InfluxDB, Kafka, NATS and ClickHouse. The homepage says it is open source under Apache 2.0.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as streaming telemetry that works: start with one command to query or change a device, then grow into a telemetry pipeline. The README describes it as a gNMI CLI client with full support for Capabilities, Get, Set and Subscribe plus collector capabilities.
brief.how_it_works: Each gNMI RPC has its own subcommand (capabilities, get, set, subscribe, with sub as a short form), and the RPC options are set through local and global flags. Targets can be given directly with -a or loaded at runtime from files, Docker, Consul or HTTP sources. In collector mode, updates pass through event processors that filter, enrich, convert and transform them before export. Prompt mode loads YANG modules so flags that take XPATH values get auto-suggestions. Configuration can come from flags, environment variables or a config file.

brief.install_notes: The homepage and README both use the one-line curl installer (bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get-gnmic.openconfig.net)"). The README also says statically linked pre-built binaries for major OS and architectures are published on the GitHub releases page. Platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows via WSL, containers, and a Kubernetes operator. Nothing in the pages mentions an account, license key or runtime needed to run the binary. Source builds need Go 1.21+ and the repo's make tooling. Your device must expose gNMI, and the examples assume user admin with a password and TLS turned off via --insecure. Real deployments need TLS configuration, which has its own docs page. Brew is the package manager the writer already knows about; the pages I read did not mention brew.
brief.standout: Prompt mode reads YANG models and turns the CLI into a path browser with auto-suggestions for XPATH flags. The project also sells itself on a 'collect once, send anywhere' pipeline: one gNMI stream feeding several outputs at once, plus a Kubernetes operator and clustering to spread targets across collectors. Its prototext output shows the raw gNMI messages going over the wire.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub page links to releases, a changelog and a CI build badge, and the docs site is versioned with a pinned toolchain in versions.env. I did not see a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so this is an inference, not a dated check.
brief.caveats: The dial-out telemetry listener is documented only for Nokia SR OS. Windows is supported only through WSL. Examples disable TLS, which is fine for a lab but not production. Source builds need Go 1.21+ and make. Prompt mode needs YANG model files cloned separately from openconfig/public. Platform and vendor support beyond these examples is not stated in what I read.

entry.title: gnmic
entry.tldr: A command-line client for gNMI, the gRPC protocol modern network gear uses to expose config and live telemetry, which can also act as a telemetry collector.
entry.deeper_look:
gnmic is a Go client for gNMI, a protocol from the OpenConfig project. Routers and switches that support it expose a gRPC endpoint. gnmic talks to that endpoint with four calls, each its own subcommand: `capabilities`, `get`, `set` and `subscribe` (`sub` for short).

The interesting one is subscribe. Instead of polling a device with SNMP, you ask for a path such as a port's statistics and the device streams updates back, for example every 10 seconds. The paths come from YANG models, the schemas that describe what a device can report or be configured with. Reading the output shows you how a vendor's internal state is laid out as a tree.

The same binary can run as a collector. It takes streams from many targets, passes them through event processors that filter, enrich and convert them, and writes the result to outputs such as Prometheus, InfluxDB, Kafka, NATS or ClickHouse. The project's pitch is "Streaming telemetry that works."

Prompt mode is a side door. Point it at a clone of the OpenConfig YANG models and the CLI suggests XPATH values as you type. The README calls this "voodoo magic", and it works as a way to browse a model without reading the schema files.
entry.install:
brew install gnmic
# You also need a device that exposes gNMI (a lab router or a vendor container image). The homepage examples assume user admin and --insecure, which turns TLS off.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands and global flags, including the target, credential and TLS options.
Asks the device which models, encodings and gNMI version it supports. Replace the address with your own lab device.
Streams port statistics from the device every 10 seconds. The path is from the homepage example and depends on the device.

entry.whats_unique: It covers both ends in one binary: a one-off CLI for poking a single device, and a collector that fans streams out to many backends. Prompt mode adds YANG-aware path suggestions.
entry.caveats: It needs a gNMI-capable device to be useful, the examples disable TLS and are lab-only, and Windows is supported only through WSL.
